statement_analysis.reason: Surat was located in the Bombay Presidency, and Mehta's dominance in the Bombay Congress machinery gave him control over session logistics including the choice of presiding officer and procedural arrangements — a decisive structural advantage.

statement_analysis.statement: Gokhale and Pherozeshah Mehta were in complete agreement on both the tactics and the timing of the expulsion of Extremists from Congress at the Surat session.
statement_analysis.reason: Gokhale was more conciliatory than Mehta and reportedly sought to preserve Congress unity. The Surat strategy of engineered expulsion was primarily Mehta's — attributing identical tactical agreement to Gokhale conflates the two figures' different temperaments and approaches.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who correctly identify Statement 1 as incorrect (recognising that Mehta was the hardliner, not the conciliator) may then accept both Statements 2 and 3 as correct without closely examining Statement 3's claim of 'complete agreement' between Mehta and Gokhale.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: Mehta was the confrontationist; Gokhale was the conciliator — Statement 1 reverses this, making it INCORRECT.
Check Statement 2: Mehta's control over Bombay Congress machinery as leverage at Surat is historically accurate — Statement 2 is CORRECT.

Check Statement 3: 'Complete agreement' between Mehta and Gokhale on tactics and timing is an overstatement — Gokhale's more conciliatory disposition means he did not fully endorse Mehta's expulsion strategy — Statement 3 is INCORRECT.
Statements 1 and 3 are incorrect — answer is (c): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits the tendency to treat 'the Moderates' as a single bloc. Mehta and Gokhale were both Moderates but had distinctly different temperaments and tactical orientations. Conflating them — as Statement 3 does with 'complete agreement' — is the standard trap. Statement 1 goes further by reversing their roles entirely. Students who have only absorbed 'Moderates vs Extremists' as a binary and have not studied the intra-Moderate dynamics will find both errors invisible.
solution.final_explanation:
The Moderate faction was not internally monolithic — Pherozeshah Mehta and Gopal Krishna Gokhale represented different temperamental and strategic orientations within the same broad tendency.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: This reverses the historical record. Mehta was the confrontationist who engineered the Extremist expulsion; Gokhale was the conciliator who sought to preserve Congress unity before Surat.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Mehta's control over the Bombay Congress machinery (Surat was in the Bombay Presidency) gave him structural dominance over the session logistics — a decisive advantage over the Extremists.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: 'Complete agreement' between Mehta and Gokhale on tactics is an overstatement. Gokhale's more moderate temperament led him to prefer compromise; the expulsion strategy at Surat was primarily Mehta's initiative.

Value Addition:
• Pherozeshah Mehta founded the Bombay Chronicle and was a leading barrister — his organisational and legal acumen made him the most effective Moderate operator.
• Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society (1905), reflecting his preference for long-term social and political work over tactical confrontation.
• The intra-Moderate divide between Mehta's hardline and Gokhale's conciliatory approaches foreshadows later Congress factional dynamics.

solution.concept_anchor: Moderate vs Extremist positions on the scope of Boycott
solution.strong_distractor: a — The scenario uses the word 'Swadeshi' prominently, and students who associate Swadeshi with the Extremist programme will select (a) without noticing that the speaker's specific argument (limiting boycott to economic goods only) is the Moderate position.
elimination_logic: Identify the speaker's actual argument: boycott should be limited to foreign goods only; government educational and judicial institutions should continue to be used.
This is the defining feature of the Moderate interpretation — economic limitation of Boycott.
Eliminate (a): The Extremist programme explicitly extended Boycott to government institutions — the speaker is arguing against this extension, not for it.
Eliminate (b): Gandhi's constructive programme involved building national institutions — unrelated to a debate about the scope of boycott in 1906.
Eliminate (d): Passive Resistance as articulated by Bipin Pal encompassed withdrawal from government institutions — the speaker is opposing this extension.

Retain (c): The Moderate position was precisely to limit Swadeshi/Boycott to economic goods and to oppose extending it to government institutions — the speaker's argument is the textbook Moderate position.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The term 'Swadeshi' in the scenario's opening line triggers the mental association with Extremism, causing students to select option (a) without carefully reading what the speaker is actually arguing. The speaker is limiting the scope of Boycott — a quintessentially Moderate position. This is a scope-extension trap: the Extremists wanted the broader scope; the Moderates insisted on the narrow (economic goods only) scope. A student who reads the scenario's opening and stops there will get this wrong.
solution.final_explanation:
The Moderate–Extremist divide over the Swadeshi and Boycott movements was fundamentally a dispute about scope — how far the boycott should extend beyond foreign manufactured goods.

In the scenario, the speaker: (i) supports promoting indigenous goods, (ii) explicitly opposes extending boycott to government schools and courts, and (iii) argues for working within British institutional frameworks. This is the precise profile of the Moderate position on Boycott.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Extremist programme called for institutional boycott (government schools, courts, titles) in addition to goods — the speaker is arguing against exactly this extension.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Gandhi's constructive programme (Swadeshi, spinning, village industries) is a later, distinct framework from the 1906 Moderate position.
• Option (c) — Correct: The Moderate interpretation of Boycott was explicitly limited to economic goods. Moderates opposed institutional boycott and continued to work within government educational and judicial structures.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Bipin Pal's Passive Resistance doctrine extended non-cooperation to government institutions — the speaker is opposing this extension, not advocating it.

Value Addition:
• The debate over scope of Boycott was the most concrete ideological battleground at the Surat session.
• Moderates feared that institutional boycott would lead to violent confrontation with the colonial state.
• The Extremist position anticipated Gandhi's Non-cooperation movement (1920–22) by fifteen years.

solution.concept_anchor: Gokhale's institutional contributions — Servants of India Society
solution.strong_distractor: c — The Deccan Education Society was associated with Gokhale's broader educational work and the Poona circle, and students who know Gokhale was connected to educational work in the Deccan region may hesitate to identify it as the odd one out.
elimination_logic: Identify the shared attribute: the question asks which is NOT an initiative or contribution associated with Gopal Krishna Gokhale.
Check (a): Servants of India Society (1905) — Gokhale founded this organisation for training selfless public workers. Clearly associated with Gokhale.

Check (b): Indian Home Rule Society — this organisation was associated with Shyamaji Krishnavarma in London (1905) and later with Annie Besant's movement; it was not Gokhale's initiative. This is the odd one out.
Check (c): Deccan Education Society — founded in 1884 by Gokhale, Tilak, and Chiplunkar in Pune for promoting modern education in Maharashtra. Gokhale was a co-founder.
Check (d): Budget speeches in Imperial Legislative Council — Gokhale was renowned for his systematic economic critique of British policy through budget speeches. Clearly his contribution.
Option (b) is the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 'Indian Home Rule Society' sounds like something Gokhale could have founded, given his constitutional nationalism and eventual support for Home Rule politics. Students who do not specifically recall that this organisation was Shyamaji Krishnavarma's London-based revolutionary body (and later associated with Besant's movement) will hesitate between (b) and (c), often selecting the latter.
solution.final_explanation:
Gokhale's institutional legacy was primarily through the Servants of India Society and his work in the Deccan educational circle.

• Option (a) Servants of India Society: Founded by Gokhale in 1905 to train dedicated public workers committed to national service. This is his signature institutional contribution.
• Option (b) Indian Home Rule Society: NOT associated with Gokhale. This was founded by Shyamaji Krishnavarma in London in 1905 as a revolutionary nationalist platform, entirely separate from Gokhale's constitutional framework.
• Option (c) Deccan Education Society: Co-founded by Gokhale, Tilak, and Vishnu Chiplunkar in Pune in 1884 to promote modern Marathi-medium education. Gokhale's involvement predates his Congress prominence.
• Option (d) Imperial Legislative Council budget speeches: Gokhale's systematic use of budget debates to expose British economic exploitation is one of his most celebrated contributions — anticipating the Drain Theory arguments in a legislative forum.

Value Addition:
• Servants of India Society members took vows of poverty and dedicated their lives to public service — a model that influenced Gandhi's own ashram movement.
• Shyamaji Krishnavarma's Indian Home Rule Society in London funded revolutionary activity including connections with Savarkar.
• Gokhale served in the Imperial Legislative Council from 1902 to 1915.

solution.concept_anchor: Post-Surat political landscape — Moderate consolidation, British response, Extremist exclusion

statement_analysis.statement: The new Congress constitution drafted after the Surat session was the primary legislative output of the Surat session itself, adopted by a unified Congress before the factions separated.
statement_analysis.reason: The new constitution was drafted AFTER the Surat session ended in disorder. It was not produced by a unified Congress at the session itself — it was a post-split Moderate consolidation measure.

statement_analysis.statement: The Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909 introduced separate Muslim electorates, which Congress initially opposed but later accepted as part of the Lucknow Pact of 1916.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1909 Reforms introduced separate Muslim electorates — a provision that Congress accepted in the Lucknow Pact (1916) as part of the Congress–Muslim League alliance. This historical progression is accurately described.

statement_analysis.statement: Following the Surat split, the Indian National Congress under Moderate control became a smaller and more ideologically homogeneous organisation, but lost its claim to represent the most assertive strands of nationalist opinion.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-Surat Congress was indeed reduced in organisational breadth and political assertiveness. The Extremists who were expelled represented the most vocal anti-imperialist voices, and their absence made Congress less dynamic as a nationalist force until the Lucknow reunification.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students may accept Statement 1 because the constitution is causally linked to the Surat session even if it was technically drafted afterwards — the temporal precision of 'adopted before the factions separated' may not be noticed.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: The new constitution was drafted AFTER the Surat session — it was not adopted at the session itself by a unified Congress. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Check Statement 2: The Morley-Minto Reforms' separate Muslim electorates and their later acceptance in the Lucknow Pact is historically accurate — Statement 2 is correct.
Check Statement 3: Post-Surat Congress becoming smaller and more homogeneous at the cost of nationalist assertiveness is an accurate historiographical assessment — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 2 and 3 correct, Statement 1 incorrect — answer is (d): 2 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1's error is a temporal precision trap — the new Congress constitution was causally connected to Surat but was not actually adopted at the Surat session itself (which ended in chaos). Students who recall 'new constitution + Surat split' as a paired fact without knowing the precise sequence will mark Statement 1 as correct and select option (c) or (d) incorrectly.
solution.final_explanation:
The post-Surat political landscape saw simultaneous Moderate organisational consolidation and British political manoeuvring.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The new Congress constitution was drafted after the Surat session ended in disorder — it was not a product of a unified session vote. The disrupted session produced no formal organisational output; the constitution was a Moderate post-split initiative.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) introduced separate Muslim electorates, which Congress initially resisted but accepted in the Lucknow Pact (1916) as the price of Congress–League political alliance.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Post-Surat Congress was stripped of its most assertive nationalists. Moderate-controlled Congress became more constitutionally careful but politically less dynamic — a period historians sometimes describe as 'moderate stagnation.'

Value Addition:
• The Morley-Minto Reforms also expanded legislative councils and allowed Indian members on the Viceroy's Executive Council — concessions designed for Moderates.
• Gokhale died in 1915, just one year before the Lucknow reunification — he did not live to see the Congress come back together.
• Post-Surat Congress struggled to maintain public relevance until the Home Rule movement revived mass engagement from 1916.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) correctly matches Tilak and Gokhale but swaps Naoroji and Bipin Pal's contributions, making it the subtlest wrong option.
elimination_logic: Anchor A (Tilak): 'Swaraj is my birthright' is unambiguously Tilak's — eliminates options (a) and (d) which misplace this attribution.
Anchor B (Gokhale): 'Political training of Indians through gradual reform' is Gokhale's defining phrase — consistent with option (b) and (c).

Confirm D (Bipin Pal): 'Passive Resistance as a political method' is Pal's distinctive contribution — option (b) correctly assigns this to Pal. The correct matching is A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap in this question swaps the intellectual contributions of Naoroji (Drain Theory) and Bipin Pal (Passive Resistance). Both are 'economic/political theory' contributions which makes the swap feel plausible — especially since Bipin Pal is less closely associated in popular memory with Passive Resistance as a distinct theoretical contribution. Students who are uncertain about Pal's specific contribution will assign the Drain Theory to him and get the last two pairings wrong.
solution.final_explanation:
This match-the-column question tests precise attribution of four different nationalist leaders to their signature intellectual or political contributions.

• A (Tilak) — matches 3 (Swaraj as birthright, festival-based mobilisation): Tilak's identity as an Extremist is inseparable from 'Swaraj is my birthright' and his use of Ganesh Chaturthi and Shivaji Jayanti.
• B (Gokhale) — matches 4 (political training, gradual constitutional reform): Gokhale's philosophy of 'political education' through constitutional engagement is his defining contribution.
• C (Naoroji) — matches 1 (Drain of Wealth Theory, foundational economic critique): Naoroji's 1901 work and the Drain thesis are indisputably his signature contribution.
• D (Bipin Pal) — matches 2 (Passive Resistance as a political doctrine): Pal was the principal theorist of Passive Resistance within the Extremist movement, articulating it as a systematic political method.

Correct matching: A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2 = option (b).

Value Addition:
• Gokhale's phrase 'political training' anticipated constitutional developments that Moderates sought through the Morley-Minto Reforms.
• Naoroji was elected to the British Parliament (1892) — an achievement he used to press India's economic case from within the British system.
• Bipin Pal's Passive Resistance is considered a theoretical ancestor of Gandhi's Satyagraha, though Gandhi developed it into a qualitatively different moral-political framework.

solution.concept_anchor: Swadeshi movement — causes, scope, social dimensions and communal tensions

statement_analysis.statement: The Partition of Bengal (1905) was the immediate trigger that energised the Swadeshi movement by exposing the limitations of Moderate petitioning and demonstrating that British authorities would proceed with unpopular policies despite constitutional protests.
statement_analysis.reason: Bengal's Partition was announced in 1905 despite widespread protests — demonstrating to nationalists that petitions alone were insufficient and directly fuelling the Extremist-driven Swadeshi and Boycott movements.

statement_analysis.statement: Both Moderate and Extremist factions within Congress fully agreed on the necessity of extending the Swadeshi programme to include the boycott of government educational institutions.
statement_analysis.reason: Swadeshi (promoting indigenous goods) was accepted by both factions, but the extension of Boycott to government educational institutions was an Extremist position that Moderates explicitly opposed. Cross-faction agreement existed only on economic Swadeshi, not on institutional boycott.

statement_analysis.statement: The Swadeshi movement contributed to early industrial nationalism in Bengal through the establishment of indigenous enterprises, including chemical and textile ventures.
statement_analysis.reason: The Swadeshi period saw the establishment of numerous indigenous enterprises in Bengal — P.C. Ray's Bengal Chemical Works, several textile mills, and other manufacturing ventures — reflecting the positive industrial dimension of the movement alongside its boycott strategy.

statement_analysis.statement: The religious and cultural symbolism deployed in the Swadeshi movement, including references to the motherland as goddess, created a sense of Muslim alienation in Bengal and contributed to early communal polarisation.
statement_analysis.reason: The heavy use of Hindu religious imagery (Vande Mataram, Durga imagery, ritual mass meetings) in the Swadeshi mobilisation was experienced by many Bengali Muslims as a culturally exclusionary Hindu nationalist idiom, contributing to the communal tensions that ultimately led to the founding of the All India Muslim League in 1906.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Only three' is the correct answer. Students who accept all four statements will select (d), but Statement 2's claim of 'full agreement' on institutional boycott is the precise error.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: Partition of Bengal 1905 as the trigger that exposed Moderate limitations — accurate; Correct.
Check Statement 2: Both factions agreeing on extending Boycott to government educational institutions — FALSE; Moderates opposed institutional boycott — Incorrect.
Check Statement 3: Indigenous enterprises (Bengal Chemical Works, textile ventures) as Swadeshi industrial output — historically documented; Correct.
Check Statement 4: Hindu religious symbolism creating Muslim alienation and contributing to communal polarisation — accurate historiographical position; Correct.
Three statements correct (1, 3, 4), one incorrect (2) — answer is (c): Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses the scope-extension trap: 'Both Moderate and Extremist factions fully agreed' on institutional boycott. 'Swadeshi' — promoting indigenous goods — did enjoy broad cross-factional support. But the statement extends this to institutional boycott, which was contested. Students who read quickly and associate 'Swadeshi = agreed by both' with the full Boycott programme will mark Statement 2 as correct and select (d).
solution.final_explanation:
The Swadeshi movement had multiple dimensions — economic, social, industrial, and communal — and testing precise knowledge of each requires distinguishing what was agreed across factions from what was contested.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Partition of Bengal 1905 as trigger exposing Moderate limitations | Correct |
| Both factions agreed on institutional boycott | Incorrect — only economic Swadeshi had cross-factional support |
| Indigenous enterprises (Bengal Chemical, textiles) as industrial Swadeshi | Correct |
| Hindu religious symbolism creating Muslim alienation | Correct |

Three statements are correct — answer is (c): Only three.

Value Addition:
• The Muslim League was founded at Dhaka in December 1906 — the same year as the Calcutta Congress session. The communal context of Swadeshi is directly related.
• P.C. Ray's Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works (founded 1901) became a flagship of Swadeshi industrialism.
• 'Vande Mataram' (from Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's 'Anandamath') was the anthem of the Swadeshi movement — its Hindu imagery became a persistent source of communal controversy.

solution.concept_anchor: Tilak's two sedition trials — 1897 and 1908 are distinct

statement_analysis.statement: Bal Gangadhar Tilak faced two separate sedition trials — one in 1897 related to his commentary on the colonial administration's famine response, and another in 1908 following the Muzaffarpur bomb case — and the sentences differed significantly in severity.
statement_analysis.reason: Tilak was prosecuted for sedition in 1897 (for writings in Kesari about the government's famine response in Maharashtra, resulting in eighteen months' imprisonment) and again in 1908 (for writings in Kesari following the Muzaffarpur bomb case, resulting in six years' transportation to Mandalay). The two trials had distinct contexts and significantly different outcomes.

statement_analysis.statement: In his 1908 courtroom defense, Tilak disavowed the use of the term 'Swaraj' and instead argued purely on the technical grounds of freedom of the press, avoiding any explicit statement of nationalist aspiration.
statement_analysis.reason: Tilak's courtroom defence in 1908 was explicitly nationalist — it is remembered precisely for his affirmation 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it.' He did not disavow nationalist aspirations; his defence was both a legal and a political statement.

solution.strong_distractor: a — This is the correct answer, but the trap is Statement 2, which contains a plausible-sounding claim. Students who vaguely recall that courtroom defences often use 'technical' legal arguments may accept Statement 2 as accurate and then incorrectly select option (c) or (d).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Two distinct sedition trials (1897 and 1908) with different contexts (famine commentary vs Muzaffarpur bomb case) and different sentences (18 months vs 6 years) — this is historically accurate; Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Tilak's 1908 defence was explicitly nationalist — his famous declaration 'Swaraj is my birthright' was made in that courtroom. He did NOT disavow Swaraj or limit himself to technical press freedom arguments — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is designed to exploit uncertainty about what exactly Tilak said in his 1908 defence. Students who do not know the specifics of the defence may assume that a lawyer-politician would use technical arguments in court rather than political declarations. The opposite is true — Tilak used his trial as a platform for nationalist assertion. The phrase 'Swaraj is my birthright' is one of the most quoted lines from any Indian nationalist court appearance.
solution.final_explanation:
Tilak's two sedition trials are a standard exam pairing that tests temporal precision and knowledge of the specific contexts of each prosecution.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 1897 trial arose from Tilak's writings in 'Kesari' about the colonial government's management of the Maharashtra famine and the killing of plague commissioner Rand — he was sentenced to eighteen months. The 1908 trial was for articles in 'Kesari' written after the Muzaffarpur bomb case — he was sentenced to six years in Mandalay. The contexts, charges, and sentences were all distinct.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Tilak did not disavow Swaraj in his 1908 defence. The trial produced his most celebrated nationalist declaration — 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it.' His defence was both legally argued and politically assertive.

Value Addition:
• The 1897 Rand assassination (for which Tilak was indirectly held responsible) was carried out by Chapekar brothers — a separate criminal act from Tilak's editorial writings.
• Tilak's 1908 jury included European jurors who voted for conviction over Indian jurors who voted for acquittal.
• Section 124A IPC (sedition) has been a controversial colonial provision — its continued applicability after independence has been a recurring constitutional debate.

solution.concept_anchor: Drain Theory — Naoroji's 1901 text and R.C. Dutt's equal contribution
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that Drain Theory is closely associated with Naoroji AND that it provided the intellectual foundation for challenging British rule may assume R accurately explains A — they know both facts and assume they are causally linked without examining whether R is actually correct as stated.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? The Drain Theory did serve as an intellectual bridge between Moderate constitutionalism (Naoroji citing it in petitions) and Extremist anti-imperialism (using it to reject British goodwill) — A is correct.

Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? R claims the theory was 'solely developed' by Naoroji. R.C. Dutt's 'Economic History of India' and Gokhale's budget speeches were equally important elaborations — the word 'solely' makes R factually incorrect.
Since A is correct and R is incorrect — correct option is (c).
Read back: A correct + R incorrect = option (c). Confirmed.
solution.final_explanation:
The Drain of Wealth Theory is so strongly identified with Naoroji that students routinely accept statements attributing it 'solely' to him without checking the qualification.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: The Drain Theory was genuinely a conceptual bridge: Moderates used it in constitutional petitions and Legislative Council speeches (Naoroji, Gokhale) to demand policy change within the British system; Extremists used it as proof that British goodwill was impossible, justifying Swaraj by self-effort. The same empirical argument thus served two different political conclusions.
• Reason (R) — Incorrect: The qualifier 'solely developed' is the fatal error. R.C. Dutt's 'Economic History of India' (two volumes, 1902–04) elaborated the Drain thesis with detailed historical analysis, and Gokhale's budget speeches provided further economic documentation. The Drain Theory was a collective Moderate intellectual project, not Naoroji's alone.

Since A is correct and R is incorrect — option (c).

Value Addition:
• R.C. Dutt's work introduced the concept of de-industrialisation — arguing that British tariff policy destroyed India's indigenous manufacturing base.
• Gokhale's budget speeches in the Imperial Legislative Council were considered the most technically sophisticated economic critiques available.
• Naoroji coined the phrase 'Un-British Rule in India' — arguing that exploitation contradicted Britain's own stated values, an appeal to British liberal conscience.

solution.concept_anchor: Events in Lajpat Rai's political life — deportation, Surat, Lucknow
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) places Lajpat Rai's deportation after the Surat session, which feels plausible because students associate his deportation with Extremist political activity during the same 1907 period without distinguishing May 1907 (deportation) from December 1907 (Surat session).
elimination_logic: Anchor the earliest event: Lajpat Rai's deportation to Mandalay was in May 1907, before the December 1907 Surat session.
The Surat session was in December 1907 — after the deportation.
Tilak's 1908 sedition sentence followed Surat.
Lucknow Congress session (reunification) was 1916 — the latest event.
Correct sequence: Deportation (May 1907) → Surat Split (December 1907) → Tilak's sedition sentence (1908) → Lucknow session (1916) = option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the close temporal proximity of Lajpat Rai's deportation (May 1907) and the Surat session (December 1907) — both in the same calendar year. Students who recall '1907 = Surat split + Lajpat Rai deportation' as a paired fact without knowing the month-level sequence will place them in the wrong order, selecting option (a). Knowing that the deportation preceded Surat (and was a Punjab agricultural issue, not a Congress outcome) is the key distinguishing fact.
solution.final_explanation:
Placing these four events in sequence requires distinguishing within-year ordering (May 1907 deportation vs December 1907 Surat) as well as the broader post-Surat timeline.

• Lajpat Rai's deportation to Mandalay: May 1907 — in response to Punjab agrarian unrest (Colonisation Bill agitation), before the Surat session.
• Surat Congress split: December 1907 — the organisational rupture.
• Tilak's sedition sentence: July 1908 — following the Muzaffarpur bomb case of April 1908 and his subsequent prosecution.
• Lucknow Congress session: December 1916 — reunification of Moderate and Extremist factions; also the occasion of the Lucknow Pact.

Correct sequence: Deportation → Surat Split → Tilak's sentence → Lucknow = option (b).

Value Addition:
• Lajpat Rai's deportation was under Regulation III of 1818 (without trial) — he was released in November 1907 after the Colonisation Bill was withdrawn.
• Tilak's 1908 sentence was delivered by a jury that included seven Europeans who outvoted five Indian members.
• The Lucknow session (1916) also produced the Lucknow Pact — Congress's agreement with the Muslim League on separate electorates and joint political demands.
